newsitem.title: GERMANY: German upper house passes Telecoms legislation.
newsitem.headline: German upper house passes Telecoms legislation.

text.p: The upper house of Germany's parliament on Friday passed revisions to legislation that regulates access to communications networks, clearing a regulatory hurdle ahead of Deutsche Telekom's share listing.
Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch welcomed the speedy handling of the matter by the upper house, controlled by the Social Democrats, main opposition in the lower house.
"I consider these changes to be acceptable," said Boetsch. "I will propose that the cabinet pass the directive in its current form."
The upper house had blocked the directive after it was passed by the lower house on September 2.
The approval of the directive guarantees that there will not be regulatory uncertainty when Deutsche Telekom lists its shares on international stock exchanges in November.

The upper house made four changes to a directive that is part of broader legislation passed earlier this month by the lower house, which is controlled by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right majority.

It affects one of the most important aspects of the bill -- the regulation which outlines how a telecommunications company must allow a competitor access to its network, so-called interconnection agreements.

Under the new directive, the network operator must grant access in the local network, even down to the local access line to the customer's home or office, and may only charge for services actually requested by the competing network operator.

All interconnection agreements must be made in written form and presented without delay to the regulator. The directive also provides for sanctions against any company that fails to provide the regulator with information in a timely fashion.
In the event of a disagreement over interconnection terms, each party may request mediation by the regulator.
If no interconnection can be reached, the regulator will be allowed after mediation to impose interconnection terms.

The changes are important because firms hoping to compete with Deutsche Telekom will have a difficult time offering services to residential customers and local businesses because most will not have local networks.
Even after full deregulation in 1998, Telekom will probably be the only telecommunications company with an extensive local network reaching millions of homes and businesses.
